title: Why do you need a skeleton?
answer: Your skeleton gives your body shape and holds it up when you stand. It gives muscles something firm to pull on when you run, wave, or chew. Some parts act like a shield. Your skull surrounds your brain, and your ribs curve around your heart and lungs. A skeleton does more than hold you together. Bones store minerals, and soft tissue inside some bones helps make new blood cells.
aliases: how many bones do you have
facts: A typical adult skeleton has 206 bones.

title: Are your bones alive?
answer: A dried bone in a museum can make it seem as if bones are just hard sticks. Inside you, each bone contains living cells. Blood travels through small channels to bring those cells supplies. The firm outer layer holds up well under pressure. Toward the inside of many bones, thin pieces of bone form a network with gaps between them. Bone cells slowly take away old bone and build fresh bone as you live.
facts: Some bone has an open pattern that looks a little like a sponge.

Why do some bones have a soft center?
How does blood reach living tissue?

title: What does bone marrow do?
answer: Deep inside some bones is soft material called marrow. Red marrow is a place where new blood cells are made. Among them are red blood cells that carry oxygen and white blood cells that help protect the body. It also makes the large cells that shed little pieces called platelets. Those pieces help stop bleeding. Yellow marrow has much more fat. Even though marrow sits inside bone, it has a supply of blood moving through it.
facts: The inside of an adult bone can contain red or yellow marrow.

questions.text: Why does your blood need red cells?
How do platelets help seal a cut?
What makes bone a living part of you?

title: How do joints let your body move?
answer: A joint is a place where bones meet. Many joints let one bone move against the other. A layer of smooth cartilage covers the touching ends in a freely moving joint. Liquid in the joint helps the surfaces slide. Strong strips called ligaments keep the bones from moving too far apart. Different joints allow different moves. Elbows mainly bend and straighten, while the joints in your shoulders let your arms move in many directions.
facts: Your elbow mainly bends and straightens like a hinge.

questions.text: What pulls on the bones at a joint?
Which joints let a bone swing in many directions?
What helps moving bones slide past each other?

title: Why can your shoulder move in so many directions?
answer: At your shoulder, the rounded top of your upper arm bone fits into a socket. Imagine a ball resting in a shallow cup. A round surface can turn in more directions than a door hinge, so you can lift your arm, sweep it forward, or make a circle. Your hip has the same general shape, but its deeper socket fits tightly around the round top of the thigh bone and helps support your weight.
facts: Your hip and shoulder both have ball-and-socket joints.

questions.text: How do the parts of a moving joint work together?
What pulls your arm into a new position?
How do bones move without rubbing roughly?

title: What is cartilage?
answer: Feel the end of your nose. It can bend a little without flopping. A tough, springy material called cartilage helps give it shape. Your outer ears contain cartilage too. The cartilage on the ends of many bones has a different job. Its surface is smooth, so it helps the bones slide in a moving joint. The ribs also meet cartilage at the front of your chest, which allows some movement as you breathe.
aliases: why is the outside of your ear bendy
facts: A smooth type of cartilage covers the ends of bones in many moving joints.

questions.text: Why is cartilage useful in a bending knee?
How is a hard bone built?
Where does cartilage help shape your chest?

title: What does your spine do?
answer: Your spine is a column made mostly of individual bones called vertebrae. Many of them are separated by firm pads that cushion the bones and allow a little movement. When a lot of small moves add up, you can bend your back. Inside the column is a passage that helps protect your spinal cord. Alongside the spine, nerves branch out to carry messages between your brain and many parts of your body.
facts: The pads between many vertebrae are called discs.

questions.text: How does your full skeleton support you?
Which bones protect the brain the spine connects to?
Where do messages going down the spinal cord start?

title: What does your skull protect?
answer: Your skull is made of several bones that fit together. Some form a strong case around your brain. Others shape your face, hold your eyes, or help support your teeth. Most of the skull stays still when you chew. Your lower jaw moves at joints near your ears. In a baby, the bones around the brain have spaces between them. These spaces help the skull grow and close gradually.
facts: The seams between some bones of the skull are called sutures.

questions.text: What happens inside the brain the skull protects?
Which column of bones protects the spinal cord?
What other bones shelter organs?

title: How does your rib cage protect you?
answer: Your ribs curve around your chest like a long set of hoops. At the back they join the spine. Many also connect to the breastbone at the front, either directly or through other pieces of cartilage. The cage helps guard soft parts inside it, including your lungs and heart. It still moves. Some muscles between the ribs lift the chest as you breathe in, helping make more room inside.
facts: Most people have twelve pairs of ribs.

questions.text: Why does making room for your lungs help you breathe?
What does the heart do inside that cage?
Where do the ribs connect in your back?

title: What is blood made of?
answer: Blood has a liquid part called plasma. It is mostly water and carries things such as dissolved nutrients and waste. Riding in it are several kinds of cells and cell pieces. Red blood cells carry oxygen. Different kinds of white blood cells help the body notice and respond to trouble. Bits called platelets help make plugs when a small blood vessel breaks. Blood has so many red cells that the mixture looks red.
facts: Plasma makes up a little over half the volume of typical blood.

questions.text: What pushes blood around your body?
Why does blood look red?
Which blood cells help defend your body?

title: How do red blood cells carry oxygen?
answer: A red blood cell is a flexible, flat disc with thinner spots in its middle. It carries a substance called hemoglobin. When the blood passes through your lungs, oxygen can attach to hemoglobin. Farther along, oxygen can come loose and move from the blood toward cells that need it. Hemoglobin contains iron and gives the red cells their color. The cells can bend as they squeeze through some very narrow blood vessels.
facts: A mature human red blood cell usually lasts about four months.

questions.text: Where does a red cell pick up oxygen?
Where are fresh blood cells made?
Which tiny tubes bring red cells close to other cells?

title: What do white blood cells do?
answer: White blood cells are part of your body’s defenses. There are several kinds with different jobs. Some can surround and break down tiny invaders or bits of dead cells. Other kinds help the body recognize things it has met before. The cells can travel in blood and can also move into the surrounding tissue. On most days you never notice them, even though they are busy checking what is happening around you.
facts: White blood cells can leave the blood and move into nearby tissues.

questions.text: What else travels through the blood?
Where does the body make new blood cells?
What barrier helps block harmful things before white cells are needed?

title: How does your blood plug a cut?
answer: If a tiny vessel is damaged, its walls can squeeze inward to slow the flow. Small bits of cells called platelets stick to the broken spot and to each other. Their group makes a plug. The blood can also produce a mesh of threads that strengthens the plug. Together these steps form a clot, which keeps more blood from escaping while the vessel and nearby skin begin to repair themselves.
aliases: why does a small cut stop bleeding
facts: Platelets are pieces that break off from much larger cells.

questions.text: Which liquid carries platelets around the body?
Where are the cells that make platelets?
What other work does skin do to protect you?

title: What are arteries and veins?
answer: Blood takes a trip through tubes called blood vessels. An artery carries blood away from the heart. The largest ones have tough walls and can stretch a bit with each beat. A vein carries blood back to the heart. Many veins, especially in arms and legs, have little flaps that help stop blood moving backward. The direction the blood moves makes a vessel an artery or a vein.
facts: Some veins have flaps that help keep blood from slipping backward.

questions.text: What gives blood the push it needs to travel?
What connects the smallest arteries and veins?
Which organs receive blood from the heart to trade gases?

title: How do capillaries deliver oxygen to cells?
answer: The larger blood vessels branch into tiny tubes called capillaries. Each tube has a very thin wall. That lets oxygen and some other materials leave the blood and reach nearby cells. Some things move the other way. Carbon dioxide can travel from cells into the blood, which later brings it to the lungs. A whole network of tiny capillaries keeps most cells close to a place where these exchanges can take place.
facts: Many capillaries are so narrow that red blood cells go through them one at a time.

questions.text: How does blood reach and leave capillaries?
What material carries the oxygen through a capillary?
Where does oxygen first get into blood?

title: What does your skin do?
answer: Skin forms a cover that helps keep water in your body and keeps many harmful things out. The surface can get scuffed, so new cells push up from below to replace old ones. A deeper layer contains tiny blood vessels, nerves, sweat glands, and the places where hairs begin. Your skin also senses what touches you. It is a living organ, and its jobs include protection, touch, and keeping your body from getting too hot.
facts: The outer layer of your skin continually sheds and replaces cells.

questions.text: What helps skin tell rough from smooth?
How does skin cool your body?
What hard parts grow from skin near your fingertips?

title: Why does sweating cool you down?
answer: Your body can make sweat when you get warm. The sweat spreads across your skin. As its water changes into a gas and mixes with the air, the change takes some heat from your skin. This cooling works best when the sweat can evaporate, rather than just roll off you. On a muggy day, the air already carries plenty of water, so sweat often evaporates more slowly and you may stay sweaty longer.
aliases: how does sweat cool the body
facts: Sweat glands send moisture to the skin through tiny openings.

questions.text: Which layers contain sweat glands?
Where else does liquid water change into a gas?
How can you sense that something is warm?

title: How do your fingernails grow?
answer: Your fingernail grows from a group of cells under the skin near the base of the nail. These cells make new nail material that slowly pushes older nail forward. The part you can trim has hardened with a tough protein called keratin. It has no nerves, which is why clipping just the free edge does not hurt. A nail protects the tender tip of your finger and gives it a firmer edge for picking things up.
facts: The visible part of a nail grows forward as new material is made near its base.

questions.text: How does skin also replace its outer surface?
What other parts of the body are made of tough keratin?
How do fingertips sense the texture of a small object?

title: Where does hair grow from?
answer: A hair gets longer from the end hidden inside the skin. That end sits in a small pocket called a follicle. Living cells near the bottom add material. By the time the hair sticks out from your head, it is mainly a strand of hardened protein. There are no nerves in that part, so a haircut does not hurt. Hairs may grow for a time, rest, then fall out as the cycle starts again.
aliases: why does a haircut not hurt
facts: Each growing hair starts in a pocket in skin called a follicle.

questions.text: What other hard part grows from cells near its base?
What else is found under the surface of skin?
How do eyelashes and tears help take care of your eyes?

title: What does your liver do?
answer: Your liver sits mostly on the right side of your belly, beneath the ribs. Blood from much of your digestive system brings it materials from food. The liver can store some supplies, change others into forms the body can use, and help handle waste. It also makes bile, a liquid that helps the small intestine handle fat. Many of these jobs happen at once, all without you having to think about them.
aliases: why do we have a liver
facts: The liver makes bile, which helps your body use fats from food.

questions.text: Where do nutrients in food enter your body?
Where can the body store the bile the liver makes?
How does the body carry nutrients to its organs?

title: What does a gallbladder do?
answer: Your gallbladder is a little pouch tucked under your liver. As the liver makes bile, some of that liquid goes to the pouch and stays there between meals. When you eat, the pouch can squeeze bile through small tubes into the first part of your small intestine. There, bile helps spread fat into smaller droplets. The smaller drops give the body’s digestive juices more surface to work on.
facts: The gallbladder fits against the underside of the liver.

questions.text: Which organ makes the bile first?

title: Why do you have a pancreas?
answer: The pancreas is a flat organ behind the stomach. It makes liquids containing helpers called enzymes. The liquid flows to the small intestine, where enzymes split food into smaller bits. The pancreas has a second job too. It releases messages called hormones into your blood. One of them is insulin, which helps many cells take in sugar from the blood. One organ can help with both the food in your gut and what travels in your blood.
facts: The pancreas sends digestive juices to the first part of the small intestine.

questions.text: What happens after food reaches the small intestine?
What other liquid goes into the intestine to help digest fats?
What is another gland that makes messages for the blood?

title: What does the thyroid do?
answer: The thyroid is a small gland near the front of your neck. It makes hormones, which are messages that move in your blood. The messages from your thyroid help tune how fast many parts of your body use energy. Thyroid hormones also help with normal growth and development. The gland needs a little of the element iodine to make these messages. It is often drawn with two halves that look like butterfly wings.
facts: The thyroid lies near the front of the neck and has a butterfly-like shape.

questions.text: Which other organ can send messages through your blood?
What small gland helps tell the thyroid when to work?
What do people mean when they say something uses energy?

title: How does your brain talk to hormone glands?
answer: A tiny gland under your brain is called the pituitary. A nearby part of your brain helps tell it what to release. Several of its messages travel in your blood and tell other glands how much to work. Others help direct growth or help your kidneys manage water. Picture a group of people passing notes. The brain can send a note to the pituitary, which then passes a message to the right place.
facts: The pituitary is roughly the size of a pea.

questions.text: How do brain cells send other kinds of messages?

What organs adjust how much water your body holds?

title: How do your eyes help you see?
answer: Light from the world enters your eye through a round opening. Clear parts near the front bend the light so it makes a sharp picture on a layer at the back. That layer is the retina. Some of its cells change incoming light into messages. A bundle of nerve fibers carries them toward your brain. Your brain combines messages from both eyes and helps you recognize the shapes, colors, and motions around you.
facts: Your retina lines the inside of the back of the eye.

questions.text: How does the eye let in more or less light?
Where does light entering the eye come from?
What turns messages from the eye into what you see?

title: Why do your pupils change size?
answer: Walk from a sunny yard into a dim room and your eyes start to adjust. The small dark opening in each eye is its pupil. A ring around it, the iris, contains muscles that can make the opening wider or narrower. A wider opening lets more light in when it is dark. In brighter light, a narrower opening limits how much enters. The change happens without needing to think about it.
aliases: why do pupils get bigger in the dark
facts: The pupil is an opening. The iris around it is the colored part of the eye.

questions.text: What happens to light after it enters the pupil?

What keeps the front surface of the eye smooth?

title: Why do your eyes make tears?
answer: Your eyes need a thin coat of liquid for more than crying. Each blink spreads a fresh layer of tears across the eye. That layer keeps the surface moist and helps it stay smooth. Tears can also wash loose dust away. Some drain through small openings in the corners of your eyes and travel down into your nose. When you cry, there may be more tears than those openings can drain, so some run down your cheeks.
aliases: why does your nose run when you cry
facts: Some tears drain into the nose through tear ducts.

title: How do taste buds tell flavors apart?
answer: When you take a bite, tiny bits of dissolved food meet taste cells. Groups of such cells form taste buds. Signals from those cells help your brain notice tastes such as sweet, bitter, or sour. Flavor includes more than these signals. The smell of food, its warmth, and how it feels in your mouth matter too. With a stuffy nose you may still taste the sweetness in a piece of fruit but have a harder time telling which fruit it is.
aliases: why does food taste different with a stuffy nose
facts: Sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and savory are five well-known kinds of taste.

questions.text: How does the nose help you tell foods apart?

How can mouth feel change what you think of as flavor?

title: How do you smell something nearby?
answer: A bowl of cut oranges can smell fresh from across a table. Some molecules leave the fruit and move through the air. When air flows through your nose, a few reach a small patch of cells high inside it. Those cells can notice certain molecules and send signals to your brain. The brain uses the pattern of signals to recognize a smell. Odors from food can also reach the same spot through the back of your mouth.
facts: Air can carry scent molecules from a food you have never touched.

questions.text: What senses work together to make a flavor?
What makes sense of messages from your nose?
How can pieces of matter small enough to go unseen reach your nose?

title: How do you feel rough and smooth things?
answer: Try brushing a finger over paper, a sweater, or the top of a table. The push on the skin changes as your finger travels over tiny bumps. Special nerve endings pick up these tiny changes. Signals move from the finger toward the brain, which puts them together to help you feel a texture. Your skin also has ways to notice heat, cold, and stronger pressure. These different signals help you feel more than just whether something is touching you.
aliases: how do you feel hot and cold
facts: Different kinds of nerve endings help you feel pressure, warmth, cold, or vibration.

Where do most touch messages go to be understood?

title: How does your body keep its balance?
answer: Your brain checks several clues to see whether you are upright or tipping. Eyes can tell you how the room is moving in your view. Sensors in muscles and joints report how bent or stretched a body part is. Small parts of the inner ear detect a turn or tilt of your head. Your brain blends these signals and tells your muscles to adjust. That is how you can stay up when the ground is uneven.
aliases: why is it easier to balance with eyes open
facts: Tiny canals in your inner ear help sense turns of your head.

title: What are carbohydrates?
answer: A potato, a pear, and a piece of bread can all provide carbohydrates. Some carbohydrates are sugars, such as the ones that help make a ripe pear sweet. Others are starches, long chains your body can break into smaller sugars. Cells can use those sugars for energy. Plant foods can also contain fiber, a kind of carbohydrate that passes much farther through your gut without being broken up by your own digestive juices.
facts: Sugars, starches, and fiber are all kinds of carbohydrates.

title: Why does your body need protein?
answer: Protein does many jobs in the body. Some proteins help form muscles. Others act like tiny tools that speed up changes inside you. When you eat foods such as eggs, fish, or beans, your gut breaks much of their protein into smaller parts. Those parts are called amino acids. Cells can join them in different orders to make the proteins they need. Think of the pieces of a train set being used to build a different sort of train.
facts: Beans, eggs, fish, nuts, and other foods can provide protein.

title: What does your body do with fat from food?
answer: Fat is a kind of nutrient found in foods such as nuts, fish, and cooking oils. It can provide energy. Some of the bits made during digestion become building materials for the outside of your cells. Fat can also help the body take in certain vitamins. Different foods contain different kinds of fat. Inside the small intestine, bile and digestive juices work together so the body can take in parts of the fat you ate.
facts: Some vitamins are easier for your body to take in when fat is present.

questions.text: What helps spread fat into tiny drops during digestion?

title: What is fiber in food?
answer: Fiber is material from plants that your body has trouble breaking down with its own digestive juices. You might eat some when you have an apple, oatmeal, or beans. Some kinds of fiber soak up water and become thick. Others can add bulk to what moves through your gut. Tiny living things in your large intestine can also use some kinds. Two foods with the same amount of fiber do not always contain exactly the same kinds of fiber.
facts: Whole grains, beans, fruits, and vegetables can provide fiber.

title: What makes a grain whole?
answer: A grain kernel has an outer coat, a part that can start a new plant, and a large store of food for that plant. A whole grain keeps all three parts. They can still be present if the grain is rolled flat or ground into flour. To make some kinds of refined flour, the mill takes away much of the outer coat and the part that would grow. This changes which kinds of nutrients and how much fiber stay in the flour.
facts: Whole oats and brown rice are examples of whole grains.

title: Why are beans useful in meals?
answer: Many of the beans people eat are seeds that grow in pods. Peas and lentils come from related plants. People use them in soups, stews, salads, and spreads. They supply protein along with fiber. That combination makes them different from foods that give you protein without fiber, such as an egg. Dried beans can be kept for later in a suitable dry place and are often cooked before eating. Some kinds also come already cooked in a can.
facts: Chickpeas, dry peas, and lentils are all foods in the legume family.

questions.text: What does your body make from parts of the protein in food?

title: Why does your body need vitamins?
answer: Vitamins are substances you need in small amounts. Different vitamins help with different jobs. Some are involved when the body builds tissue or changes food into forms it can use. Although vitamins help the body use food, they are not a source of energy like sugar or fat. Foods contain different mixtures of vitamins. Some vitamins dissolve in water, while others dissolve in fat. That difference affects how the body takes them in and keeps them.
facts: The body can take in some vitamins with the help of fat.

title: What does vitamin C do?
answer: Vitamin C helps your body make an important protein for skin and other tissues. It can also help your body take in iron from some plant foods. That is one reason foods with vitamin C can be useful as part of a varied meal. An orange is a familiar example, but it is far from the only source. Other fruits and some vegetables contain vitamin C as well. People need to get it from what they eat or drink.
facts: Bell peppers and oranges are examples of foods that can provide vitamin C.

title: How does vitamin D help bones?
answer: Vitamin D helps your gut take in calcium from food. Calcium is one of the materials your body uses to build strong bones and teeth. Some foods, such as several kinds of fish, naturally contain vitamin D. It may be added to other foods, and your skin can also make some when sunlight reaches it. Vitamin D and calcium do different jobs. One helps calcium get into the body, and the other becomes part of the hard material in bones.

facts: Some foods contain added vitamin D.

title: Why is calcium important for bones?
answer: Calcium is a mineral nutrient. Inside your body, much of it goes into the hard material in bones and teeth. It has other jobs too. A small amount travels through the blood and helps nerves send messages and muscles move. Calcium can come from foods such as yogurt, certain greens, or drinks with calcium added. The amount in a serving can depend on the particular food. Your body uses calcium over time as it maintains living tissue.
facts: Most of the calcium in your body is found in your bones and teeth.

questions.text: What vitamin helps you take calcium in from your food?

Where do bones keep many of their minerals?

title: Why does your body need iron?
answer: Iron is a metal that can be part of materials in your body, even though it does not look like a nail or a piece of steel there. Red blood cells use it in hemoglobin, which picks up oxygen as blood flows past the lungs. Iron in food helps supply what the body needs for jobs like this. Foods such as beans, meat, and some cereals with added iron can provide it in different forms.
facts: Iron is part of the oxygen-carrying protein hemoglobin.

Which pod seeds can provide iron in a meal?

title: Why does your body need water?
answer: Water is part of your blood and of the cells all through your body. It helps carry materials and helps you stay at a workable temperature. You lose water in sweat, in urine, and from the air you breathe out. What you drink and some of what you eat can replace it. You might notice that you feel thirsty after running around on a warm day. Your body uses more than one clue to keep the amount of water it holds in balance.

facts: Water leaves your body in ways you can see, such as sweat, and in the air you breathe out.

questions.text: How can water on your skin carry away heat?

title: What can a food label tell you?
answer: Foods sold in many packages have a Nutrition Facts label. It lists certain materials in a stated amount of food, such as its fiber, protein, or iron. The list helps you compare foods if you pay attention to how much food the numbers describe. Two packages might use different serving sizes. A separate list of ingredients tells you what went into the food. The label can answer some useful questions even though it cannot tell you whether you will like the food.

answer: The serving size on a Nutrition Facts label tells you how much food the numbers refer to. It might be a cup, several crackers, or another amount. title: What does sleep do for you?
answer: When you sleep, you are less aware of the things around you, but your body and brain keep working. Your brain goes through several kinds of sleep in a repeating pattern. Sleep helps with memory and attention, so it can be harder to concentrate after a night of poor rest. Your body does many ordinary upkeep jobs while you sleep too. How much sleep a person needs changes as they grow, and the hours you are in bed do not always match the hours you are asleep.
facts: Several kinds of sleep repeat during a typical night.

title: How does moving your body help it work well?
answer: When you move enough to breathe faster, your heart and lungs are moving more oxygen around your body. Over time, regular movement can help them do those jobs well. Moving your body also makes muscles work. Some activities, such as running and hopping, give your bones a reason to keep building strong material. Movement comes in many forms. Playing an active game, walking, and dancing are everyday ways to use your muscles and practice moving with control.
facts: Walking, dancing, and many kinds of play can all count as physical activity.

questions.text: How does your heart move blood to working muscles?

title: What does handwashing wash away?
answer: A hand can look clean and still have material from things it touched. Some of that material clings to natural oils on the skin. Water alone may run over it without carrying it all away. Soap helps loosen oily material, and rubbing reaches folds and spots such as the skin between your fingers. Rinsing carries away the loosened material. That is why soap, rubbing, and rinsing each have a job in the same wash.
facts: Soap and rubbing help loosen material before water rinses it away.

questions.text: What is the surface you are cleaning made of?
Why do your hands feel smooth or rough at different times?
What helps the body guard against some invaders that get inside?

title: What protects the outside of a tooth?
answer: The part of a tooth that sticks above your gums wears a hard coat called enamel. It is tough enough to protect the tooth through lots of biting and chewing. Some bacteria in the mouth can make acids when they use sugars and starches. Over time, repeated contact with those acids can take minerals out of enamel. If enough damage adds up, a hole called a cavity can form. Fluoride can help teeth resist this kind of damage.
aliases: what does fluoride do for teeth
facts: The hard outer coat on the part of a tooth you can see is called enamel.

Why does breaking food into small pieces help digestion?

title: What is DNA?
answer: Many of your cells hold a long, thin material called DNA. Its smaller parts can be thought of as four kinds of letters. The order of those parts carries information. Some stretches help tell cells how to make materials they need, and some help control when instructions are used. Much of your DNA contains information you inherited from your biological parents. The thread is so fine that you cannot see a single strand just by looking.

title: What is a cell in your body?
answer: Your body is built from tiny living units called cells. Most are too small to see without a tool that makes them look bigger. Different cells do different work. A nerve cell can carry a message over a distance, and some muscle cells can shorten when called on to move you. Cells are grouped together into tissues. Several tissues can work together in an organ, which is how small living parts help a body do large jobs.

title: What holds the inside of a cell together?
answer: The outer surface of a human cell is a very thin layer called its membrane. It separates the watery inside from the area around the cell. It also helps control what goes in and out. Some materials can pass through the thin layer. Others need help getting across. The membrane is more than a bag for holding things. It helps a cell get what it needs while keeping its inside different from the place around it.

title: What is the nucleus of a cell?
answer: Many of the cells in your body have a small part called the nucleus. It has its own border inside the cell. Most of that cell’s DNA is kept there. The cell can use information from DNA when it needs to make materials or get ready to divide. Different kinds of cells use different portions of the information. A cell in your skin can do a different job from one in your muscle even though they hold much of the same DNA.

title: How do chromosomes help pack DNA?
answer: DNA is long and thin, and a cell is tiny. To pack DNA into that small space, the cell winds it around proteins and folds it further. A piece of DNA and the proteins that help pack it form a chromosome. Chromosomes are especially easy to tell apart after they tighten up as a cell gets ready to divide. Many of your cells have two sets, with one set inherited from each biological parent.

title: What is a gene?
answer: A gene is a stretch of DNA that carries information a cell can use. Many genes have directions for making a protein, such as one that forms part of a cell or helps it do a job. Some genes help in other ways. A cell does not need to use every gene all the time. A muscle cell and a skin cell can turn to different directions. That can help explain why they do different work even though they both belong to you.
facts: Some genes help a cell make a protein, and some have other jobs.

title: What is a genome?
answer: The full collection of inherited instructions in a living thing is its genome. If you think of a gene as one passage in a big set of books, the genome is the full set. Some parts give information for making proteins. Other parts help run and organize the collection. Plants, animals, and other living things each have genomes. Two people have very similar human genomes, though there can be many small differences between their versions.
aliases: all the DNA of an organism
facts: A genome can contain information besides the parts that give instructions for proteins.

title: How can people have different versions of a gene?
answer: Imagine looking up the same short passage in two copies of a book and finding a letter that is different. A related thing can happen in DNA. At a certain place, one person may carry a slightly different version from another person. Scientists call each version at that place an allele. Some differences can affect a trait, while others have little or no effect you can see. Often, more than one place in the DNA matters for the same trait.

title: What are traits?
answer: A trait is something you can notice or measure about a living thing. The color of a flower and a person’s height are examples. Information you inherit can help shape many traits, but what happens as you grow can matter too. A plant with the same inherited directions may grow differently in a sunny place than in a dark one. Your ability to read a particular book also depends on learning, even though your body has traits that help you see or hear.

title: Do genes decide exactly how tall you will be?
answer: One gene cannot tell you exactly how tall you will become. Lots of small differences in inherited information can influence how a person grows. Food, health, and other parts of life during childhood can also make a difference. Siblings can inherit different sets of information from the same biological parents and grow to different heights. People also grow at different times. The order of heights among classmates today may look different after everyone has finished growing.

title: How does one cell become two?
answer: As you grow, the number of cells in your body goes up. One way it happens is that a cell copies its DNA and gets the two matching sets ready to move apart. In a process called mitosis, those sets move into two separate groups. The first cell then splits, leaving two cells with a set of instructions each. The body can use this process to grow and to replace worn cells. Some parts of the body replace cells much faster than others.

facts: Cells copy their DNA before making two cells in this kind of division.

title: What makes some twins identical?
answer: Identical twins come from one fertilized egg that begins developing and divides into two groups of cells. This gives them almost the same DNA from the beginning. They may look a lot alike and can still be different because each grows and has individual experiences. Fraternal twins start from two separate eggs joined separately with sperm, so each begins with a different mixture of family DNA. They are related in the ordinary way full brothers or sisters are, even though they are born around the same time.
aliases: why do identical twins look alike
facts: Fraternal twins start from two different fertilized eggs.

title: Why is DNA compared to a twisted ladder?
answer: Think of a ladder with two long sides and rungs in between. A DNA molecule has two sides made of repeating parts. Each rung is a pair of smaller pieces. A piece called A pairs with T, and G pairs with C. The whole ladder coils around itself, so it looks twisted. That shape helps explain how one side of DNA can help a cell work out what belongs on the other side.

title: What are mitochondria?
answer: In many of your cells are small parts called mitochondria. They help turn energy from food into a form other parts of the cell can use. A muscle cell needs a strong supply when it works, and its mitochondria help provide that supply. The parts are often shown as shapes with folds inside. They even have a little of their own DNA, although most of a person’s DNA is kept elsewhere in cells.
facts: Muscle cells have a need for many supplies of usable energy.

title: Do your cells have DNA outside the nucleus?
answer: Most of the DNA in a body cell stays in the nucleus. There is also a small amount in some little cell parts called mitochondria. These parts help the cell make energy available for use. Their DNA carries information used there. The way people usually inherit this smaller set is also different. It is usually passed through the biological mother, while the larger sets of chromosomes in the nucleus usually come from both biological parents.
facts: Scientists often shorten mitochondrial DNA to mtDNA.

title: What is computer hardware?
answer: A screen, a keyboard, and the pieces inside a laptop are all hardware. Hardware is the physical part of a computer. Some pieces let you send in information, as when you press a key. Others can show or play a result. The parts deep inside do work such as following instructions or storing an image. Computers come in many shapes, but they need pieces built to carry out jobs their programs ask for.
facts: A phone and a desktop computer both contain processors and memory.

questions.text: What tells these physical parts what to do?

title: What is software?
answer: If you can use one tablet to draw and then play a game, it is because different software runs on the same equipment. Software includes instructions that the computer can follow. A drawing app tells it how to react when you drag a finger, while a music app tells it how to play sound. Other software helps those apps talk to the parts inside. New instructions can change what a computer does without replacing the physical machine.
facts: Programs can turn the same physical device into a drawing tool, a music player, or a game.

title: What does a computer processor do?
answer: A processor is a chip that follows many simple instructions very quickly. One instruction might ask it to add two numbers. Another might tell it to compare them or get a piece of information from memory. A long series of such acts can help a game decide whether two shapes touched. Usually more than one part of the machine helps with a large job. The processor leads much of the step-by-step work your programs ask for.
facts: CPU is short for central processing unit.

title: How does computer memory hold what you are using?
answer: Think of your desk while you work. You may set out just the books and papers you need right now. A computer has a work area called RAM. It holds instructions and a copy of some information that programs are using. The processor can reach that space quickly. If you turn the computer off, most kinds of RAM forget what they held. Saving moves a lasting copy to a different part of the machine.

title: How do computers keep files without power?
answer: A computer keeps some information in devices that are built to remember without power. They can hold drawings, recordings, and programs between uses. A hard drive stores information with magnetism on spinning surfaces. A solid-state drive uses chips instead. When you open a saved drawing, the computer reads the stored information and can place a working copy in faster memory. Changes still need to be saved if you want to find them later.

title: What is an operating system?
answer: An operating system is a set of programs that helps a computer run. It can give apps a way to open files, read keys, play sounds, or draw on the screen. answer: Some computer questions have two possible answers. A door is open or it is not. A player has a key or does not. Boolean logic lets a program work with true and false answers like these. It can put several answers together to make a longer test. The programmer needs to know exactly what each check means. answer: Imagine a pretend treasure chest that opens only when you have a key and stand on a marked square. You need both parts. Having just the key does not open it, and standing on the square alone does not open it either. A computer can combine the two checks using an AND rule. It gets a true result when both checks are true together. That result can then tell the game to open the chest.

title: When does an OR rule say yes?
answer: Suppose a pretend gate opens if you have a round token or a square token. With either token the gate opens. If you have both, it can open too. This is the usual OR rule in computing. A true result means at least one part of the test is true. People sometimes say “or” when they mean you must choose just one thing. In logic, there is a different rule for allowing exactly one.

title: What does NOT do to a logic value?
answer: If a light is on, the sentence “the light is not on” is false. If the light is off, that sentence is true. The logic rule NOT flips a true-or-false answer. It is useful when a program needs to check the opposite of a question it can already ask. A game that knows whether its menu is open might also want to know whether the menu is not open, so it can let a player move.

title: What rule means one or the other, but never both?
answer: An imaginary sign might light up when only one person presses a button. If neither presses a button, it stays dark. If both press at once, it also stays dark. That rule is called XOR, or exclusive OR. It has only two ways to get a true answer with two buttons. Exactly one of the two buttons must be pressed. This is different from the usual OR rule, where pressing both would also turn the sign on.

title: What can a truth table show you?
answer: A truth table is a chart for checking a logic rule. Suppose a sign responds to two buttons. You can make one row for neither button pushed, one for only the first, one for only the second, and one for both. Then write what the sign does in every row. A table helps reveal an answer you might have missed. Programmers and engineers can use it to compare rules before they write a program or build a circuit.

title: How can a program put a list in order?
answer: To order a pile of numbered cards, you could make a short row and slide each new card into its place. If the row says 2, 4, and 8, a new card with 5 goes after 4. title: How can a program find something in a sorted list?
answer: Think of looking for the number 82 in a long row of cards already in order. You can look at the card in the middle. If it is 50, you can skip all the lower cards because 82 must be farther right. Look at the new middle of that remaining part and make the same decision. In a binary search, each step narrows the choices to about half of what came before. You cannot do that safely if the cards are scrambled.
